summary: Describes the ECN-nonce, an optional addition to Explicit Congestion Notification. It guards against a receiver accidentally or deliberately hiding congestion marks from the TCP sender. This RFC is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: The ECN-nonce gives a TCP sender a check on whether a receiver reports congestion marks. A mark erases a bit the receiver needs to calculate its report, so a hidden mark may make the report wrong.

questions: how does the tcp ns flag work
how can a tcp sender detect a cheating receiver
subtitle: A TCP nonce sum designed to reveal hidden ECN congestion marks.

tldr.problem: Explicit Congestion Notification depends on a receiver echoing congestion marks, but a buggy receiver or a middlebox could hide those marks.
tldr.mechanism: The sender places a one-bit nonce in each ECN-capable packet. The receiver reports the running one-bit sum in a TCP flag, while a congestion mark erases the original nonce.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Historic. It says the ECN-nonce had not been widely deployed when the memo was written.

facts.label: TCP flag
facts.value: NS, bit 7 of the Reserved field

facts.label: Chance to catch a concealed mark

today: RFC 3540 is marked Historic in the unit metadata. Its June 2003 text says the ECN-nonce had not been deployed widely at that time.

sections.title: Why Add a Nonce to ECN
sections.content:
Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) asks a receiver to echo congestion experienced by packets. RFC 3540 describes a risk: a receiver, a NAT, a firewall, or another device could remove the congestion signal and conceal it from the TCP sender.

The ECN-nonce adds one TCP header flag and uses the two ECN-capable transport codepoints to carry a random bit. The RFC says the optional mechanism is intended to help detect concealed marks and drops; it had not been widely deployed at publication.
sections.plainLanguage: ECN only helps a sender react to congestion if the receiver reports the marks it sees. The nonce gives the sender a way to check that report.

sections.title: How the Nonce Sum Works
sections.content:
For each ECN-capable packet, the sender encodes a nonce of zero as ECT(0) or one as ECT(1). The receiver keeps the one-bit sum, or parity, of nonce bits over the acknowledged byte range and returns it in the TCP Nonce Sum (NS) flag.

A congested router changes the ECN field to Congestion Experienced (CE), replacing the nonce. The receiver then cannot know that bit and may report a different sum. Each unchecked acknowledgement gives the sender a 50-50 chance of detecting an intentionally concealed mark.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver reports a one-bit total for the data it acknowledges. If a router marks a packet, the mark replaces its nonce, so the receiver may no longer be able to report the correct total.

sections.title: Checking and Resynchronizing
sections.content:
The receiver returns its current nonce sum in each acknowledgement. The sender compares that value with the sum it expected, except while handling an ECN-Echo congestion signal. Retransmissions are not ECN-capable and carry no nonce.

After a mark or loss, the sender and receiver sums can differ. Once congestion recovery allows checking again, the sender resets its expected sum to the receiver's value. The sender's response to an incorrect sum is a policy choice; the RFC suggests it could react as it does to an ECN-Echo signal.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender compares the receiver's total with its own expected total. After a congestion event, it can copy the receiver's value so later reports can be checked again.

sections.title: The NS Flag and Limits
sections.content:
The NS flag occupies bit 7 of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) Reserved field, next to the ECN-Echo and Congestion Window Reduced flags. Its initial sum is one, and the handshake carries that value so peers can infer support; this is not a negotiation.

The nonce is not a cryptographic integrity check for the connection. The RFC says the bit sequence should not come from a predictable generator such as a linear-feedback shift register. It also notes that disabled Path MTU discovery can allow a receiver to reconstruct a nonce from unmarked fragments, reducing protection.
sections.plainLanguage: The nonce sum uses a reserved TCP header bit. It can expose hidden congestion marks, but it does not protect the overall connection from tampering.
